questions.question: Describe Romantic theory of love. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Romantic Theory of love.
  • Answer: (Mark can be awarded to both theories of love - Sternberg’s
  • Triangular Theory as well as Romantic love as attachment.)
  • Sternberg’s triangular theory of love: Robert Sternberg’s (1986,
  • 1988, 2006) triangular theory of love posits that all love experiences are
  • made up of three components: intimacy, passion, and commitment.
  • • Intimacy: Feelings of warmth, (bond) closeness, connection, and
  • sharing.
  • • Passion: Intense feelings, both positive and negative, including
  • sexual desire, excitement, and other strong emotions related to
  • attraction and romance.
  • • Commitment: The decision to maintain the relationship, even
  • through difficulties
  • Eight different types of love from different combinations of these 3
  • components. They are: 1. Non love - All 3 components are absent ; 2.
  • Liking- Intimacy alone;3. Infatuation- Passion alone; 4. Empty Love-
  • Commitment alone; 5. Romantic Love- Intimacy + Passion; 6. Fatuous
  • Love - Passion + Commitment ; 7. Companionate Love - Intimacy +
  • Commitment; 8. Consummate Love - Intimacy + Passion +
  • Commitment
  • OR
  • Romantic love as attachment : Hazan and Shaver’s Attachment
  • Theory- Refer Q No. 23
  • [U] / [CO1]

questions.question: What is Interdependence (Social Exchange) Theory, and how does it explain relationship maintenance? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What is Interdependence Theory (Social Exchange Theory) and how does it explain relationship maintenance?
  • Answer: Interdependence or Social Exchange Theory (Harold Kelley
  • & John Thibaut) postulates that interpersonal relationships are
  • governed by perceptions of the rewards and costs exchange d in
  • interactions. Rewards include such things as emotional support, status,
  • and sexual gratification (in romantic relationships); Costs are such
  • things as the time and energy that a relationship requires.
  • The interactions between acquaintances, friends, a nd lovers will
  • continue as long as the participants feel that the benefits they derive
  • from the relationship are reasonable in comparison to the costs of being
  • in the relationship. Individuals assess their satisfaction with a
  • relationship by comparing the relationship outcomes (rewards minus
  • costs) to their subjective expectations.
  • Relationship maintenance involves the actions and activities used to
  • sustain the desired quality of a relationship. They can be: Spontaneous
  • (e.g., checking in, shared meals) or Intentional (e.g., visiting
  • family/friends). Both spontaneous and intentional maintenance
  • activities are linked to relationship satisfaction and commitment .
  • Relationship satisfaction is higher when the frequency of maintenance
  • behaviours aligns with expec tations or when contributions are
  • perceived as equitable.
  • [U] / [CO1]
